In dark mode this makes the background a variant of `$secondary` while the text remains `$secondary`, so the text and background become very similar shades, plausibly causing unreadable/low-contrast badge text.

This is the same underlying concern raised in the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: mobile/topic-post.scss:182 (h3) light value changed from 20% to 50%, diverging from desktop/topic-post.scss:321 which keeps 20%

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `mobile/topic-post.scss` `a.star h3` changing from `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)` to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`, which does raise the primary lightness from 20% to 50%. In `desktop/topic-post.scss`, the corresponding `a.star h3` remains at primary lightness 20% (`dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%), ...)`). This is a real, diff-grounded inconsistency, but it’s primarily a visual/design divergence rather than a clearly verifiable functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ~80 hand-written repetitions of dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: X%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 100-X%)) should be abstracted into a mixin/function (like existing dark-light-diff) to eliminate mechanical pairing errors

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces many repeated patterns like `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: X%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: Y%))` across numerous SCSS files. This repetition is clearly diff-grounded and creates maintainability risk: several instances already vary from the implied mechanical rule (e.g., `desktop/topic-post.scss` changes an `a` color to `$primary` lightness 70 with `$secondary` 30, and `mobile/modal.scss` uses `$primary` 30 with `$secondary` 70), illustrating how easy it is to introduce inconsistent pairings. Abstracting into a helper function/mixin would reduce duplication and prevent such inconsistencies, but this is not by itself a directly verifiable functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Inconsistent hand-tuning of complementary pairs (e.g. admin_base.scss:506 uses 40%/60%, header.scss:196 uses 30%/70%) undermines the systematic pairing convention; deviations should be documented if intentional

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show multiple dark-light-choose pairs with different lightness values (e.g., admin_base.scss uses 40%/60%, header.scss uses 30%/70%), but the claim that this “undermines” a “systematic pairing convention” is not verifiable from the diff itself—no convention or rule is defined or referenced here. The changes consistently use complementary-looking pairs (often summing to 100), so calling them inconsistent in a problematic way is speculative/design-opinion rather than a concrete, diff-provable issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Trailing whitespace introduced at admin_base.scss:726 and desktop/queued-posts.scss:14

adjudication.rationale: The diff does not clearly show any end-of-line trailing whitespace at the cited locations (admin_base.scss around the `.description` rule and desktop/queued-posts.scss `span {color: ...; }`). Even if minor spacing were present, trailing whitespace would be a formatting nit rather than a verifiable functional defect from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: .small-action a in desktop/topic-post.scss: light argument changed from scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%) to 70%, silently making usernames/links in small actions low-contrast in light themes; looks like a copy-paste swap of arguments

adjudication.rationale: In `app/assets/stylesheets/desktop/topic-post.scss`, the diff changes a bold link color from `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)` to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%))` (see the hunk around the `.arrow` rule). This makes the *light-theme* branch use `$primary` at 70% lightness instead of 30%, unlike the other changes in this PR which generally preserve the original light-theme lightness and only adjust the dark-theme branch. That asymmetry strongly suggests an argument/lightness mix-up that would reduce contrast in light themes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: .name in desktop/user.scss and mobile/user.scss: light argument changed from scale-color($primary, 30%) to 50%, erasing the intentional visual hierarchy between the darker name and lighter title on user cards in light themes

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in both `app/assets/stylesheets/desktop/user.scss` and `app/assets/stylesheets/mobile/user.scss` that `.name` color was changed from `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)` to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`, while `.title` remains at a 50% lightness choice. This makes `.name` and `.title` effectively the same color in light mode, removing the previous darker-vs-lighter distinction. Whether that hierarchy was “intentional” is not provable from the diff alone, but the loss of contrast is a concrete, diff-grounded UX concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Embedded link h3 in mobile/topic-post.scss: light argument changed from scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%) to 50%, breaking the h3/h4 hierarchy and diverging from the desktop equivalent which kept 20%

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in `app/assets/stylesheets/mobile/topic-post.scss` within `a.star { h3 { ... } }` the color changed from `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)` to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`, i.e., the primary lightness went from 20% to 50%. In the corresponding desktop file `app/assets/stylesheets/desktop/topic-post.scss`, `a.star h3` uses `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 80%))`, so mobile now diverges from desktop. Whether this “breaks hierarchy” is a UI/consistency concern rather than a clearly verifiable functional defect, but it is specific and grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: .custom-message-length in mobile/modal.scss: light and dark arguments appear swapped relative to desktop modal's (70%, 30%) — light themes get nearly black hint text and dark themes get very light text, an argument-order bug

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, desktop/modal.scss sets `.custom-message-length` to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%))`, but mobile/modal.scss sets it to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%))`. This reverses the light/dark lightness intent compared to the consistent pattern elsewhere in the diff (70% for $primary in light theme, 30% for $secondary in dark theme), so it likely makes the hint too dark in light mode and too light in dark mode.

adjudication_records.issue_text: embed.css.scss uses dark-light-choose and $secondary, which may not be defined in the standalone embed compile pipeline, risking compile failure or wrong output; worth verifying the function is available for embedded contexts

adjudication.rationale: In app/assets/stylesheets/embed.css.scss the diff changes `color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%);` to `color: dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%));`. This newly introduces a dependency on the `dark-light-choose(...)` Sass function and on `$secondary` in the embed stylesheet. The diff alone cannot confirm whether the embed compilation context includes those definitions/variables, so it’s not a verifiable defect from the patch itself, but it is a concrete, diff-grounded risk worth checking.
